intro: Games once belonged to one town, one temple or one school. This unit follows two ways they became bigger. The first is the Olympic Games. A festival at Olympia in Greece became, after 1894, a stage where nations march behind flags. Federations wrote shared codes so athletes from different countries could meet under one set of rules.

The second is a law. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 is one sentence about education. It never names a sport. Yet it changed who gets a spot on a school team. In Illinois, the IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling champions in 1937 and held its first girls wrestling state finals in 2022.

In this unit you will read dates, laws, court cases and records. You will be able to explain who wrote a rule, who was shut out and when a door opened. You will also be able to weigh an argument, like whether a country should boycott the Games.
bigQuestion: Who decides who gets a place on the roster, and how do flags, codes and laws change that answer?

test.q: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?
test.why: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus in southern Greece.

test.q: What did the June 1894 congress at the Sorbonne create?
test.why: The 1894 congress founded the IOC and chose Athens for 1896.

test.q: Why do international federations matter to the Olympics?
choices: They keep one rule book for each sport so nations can meet.
test.why: Each federation writes one code for its sport and runs it at the Games.

test.q: Which lesson does Jim Thorpe's story teach about the amateur rule?
choices: It was written by Title IX.
It could take medals from an athlete who had been paid to play.
test.why: Thorpe lost his 1912 medals in 1913 because he had been paid to play baseball.

test.q: When did the rings flag first fly at the Games?
test.why: Coubertin designed it in 1913, and it first flew at Antwerp in 1920.

test.q: Which Games did the United States lead a boycott of?
test.why: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, the U.S. led a boycott of Moscow in 1980.

test.q: Why was the IOC's choice of Berlin argued about in the 1930s?
choices: Germany refused to use the rings flag.
The Nazi government pushed Jewish athletes out of German sport.
Berlin was too far from Athens.
test.why: After 1933 the Nazi government excluded Jewish athletes, and a boycott movement grew.

test.q: What happened to Chicago's Olympic hopes in 1904 and 2016?
choices: It won the 1904 vote but lost the Games to St. Louis, and it lost the 2016 vote.
test.why: The 1904 Games moved to St. Louis, and Chicago went out in the first round of the 2016 vote.

choices: sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money
separate teams for boys and girls
test.why: Title IX bans sex discrimination in federally funded education programs.

test.q: How is Title IX different from the Olympic Charter?
choices: Title IX is a rule book for the Games; the charter is a U.S. law.
Title IX is a U.S. law; the charter is the IOC's rule book.
test.why: Congress passed Title IX in 1972. The IOC writes the Olympic Charter.

test.q: Which agency wrote the first Title IX regulations in 1975?
choices: the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare
test.why: HEW wrote the regulations, which took effect on July 21, 1975.

test.q: Which sport do the Title IX regulations name as a contact sport?
test.why: The regulations name wrestling with boxing, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball.

test.q: Which body ran women's college championships from 1971 to 1982?
test.why: The AIAW ran women's college championships until it closed in 1982.

test.q: Which year saw the first IHSA boys wrestling state champions?
test.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900 and crowned its first boys wrestling champions in 1937.

test.q: What changed for Illinois girls wrestlers in the 2021–22 season?
choices: The IHSA added a girls wrestling state series, with the first finals in 2022.
Girls were barred from boys' teams.
test.why: The IHSA added girls wrestling for 2021–22 and held the first girls state finals in 2022.

write.prompt: Which changed who gets on the roster more: the Olympic codes and flags, or Title IX? Argue your answer using two or three records from this unit, such as the Olympic Charter, the 1980 boycott, the text of Title IX, the 1975 regulations or the IHSA's 2022 girls finals.
tips: Name each document or record you use and give its year.
Say who wrote each rule: the IOC, a federation, Congress, an agency or the IHSA.
Name who was shut out before a change and when the door opened.
Compare the two paths instead of only praising one.
Use unit words such as code, boycott, regulation and state series.
